formation.title: The Restoration of Nubia
formation.text:
The scattered Nubian lands are united once more. For centuries, the kingdoms of Makuria and Alodia channeled the wealth of Africa northward along the Nile, their archers the terror of any who dared invade, their churches adorned with paintings that rivaled Constantinople. Though those kingdoms fell to internal strife and foreign pressure, the Nubian people endured. Now a new chapter begins. Will Nubia restore itself as a military power whose bowmen make empires tremble, or as the indispensable trade corridor linking Africa's riches to the wider world?

This choice unlocks a destiny path in the Traditions tab.

options.text: We are the heirs of Ta-Seti: let our arrows darken the sky.

modifiers.name: Land of the Bow
modifiers.text: The ancient Egyptians called this land Ta-Seti, the Land of the Bow. For millennia, Nubian archers were feared across the ancient world, employed as mercenaries from Egypt to Persia. Now, as Nubia rises again, its warrior traditions are reborn. The bow is more than a weapon; it is the symbol of a people who have never been truly conquered.

options.text: Gold, ivory, and incense: the Nile shall carry our fortune.

modifiers.name: The Golden Corridor
modifiers.text: Nubia sits astride the only secure route between sub-Saharan Africa and the Mediterranean, the Nile corridor. Gold, ivory, ebony, incense, and exotic animals flow north through Nubian hands, while grain, linen, and manufactured goods flow south. The kingdom that controls this corridor controls the wealth of two worlds.

advances.name: Ta-Seti Archery
advances.text: The bowmen of Ta-Seti, the 'Land of the Bow', were feared across the ancient world. This tradition of archery excellence endures in Nubian warriors who train from childhood with the great longbow.

advances.name: Wadi Allaqi Gold
advances.text: The gold deposits of Wadi Allaqi and the Eastern Desert have been a source of Nubian wealth since the age of the pharaohs. Systematic mining operations extract the precious metal that funds kingdoms.

advances.name: Saqia Irrigation
advances.text: The ox-driven waterwheel, the saqia, transforms the narrow Nile floodplain into productive farmland, turning the desert green one field at a time.

event.title: The Saqia Transforms the Nile
event.text: The saqia, the ox-driven waterwheel, revolutionized Nubian agriculture. Unlike in Egypt, where the Nile's annual flood irrigates the land naturally, Nubian agriculture depends entirely on mechanical irrigation. A single saqia, turning through the day, can water two hectares of cropland from the river's edge. As saqias multiply along the Nile, villages expand, populations grow, and the narrow strip of green along the river banks widens. The rhythmic creaking of the waterwheel has become the heartbeat of Nubian life.

options.text: The river gives life to all who know how to draw from it.

advances.name: Nubian Painted Pottery
advances.text: Nubian potters produce distinctive wares decorated with Christian symbols (fish, doves, crosses, and palm fronds) in styles that blend African and Mediterranean traditions.

advances.name: Nile Corridor Trade
advances.text: Nubia commands the Nile corridor, the only secure route for African exotica to reach the Mediterranean. Ivory, ebony, incense, and exotic animals pass through Nubian hands.

advances.name: Coptic Roots
advances.text: Nubia's conversion to Christianity before 600 AD established deep connections to Coptic Egypt and the wider Christian world, creating a spiritual heritage that persists across centuries.

advances.name: Nile Fortifications
advances.text: Fortified cities and watchtowers line the Nile, protecting Nubian settlements from desert raiders and foreign invaders. These stone fortresses control the river's chokepoints.

advances.name: Pitati Bowmen
advances.text: The Pitati were elite Nubian archer contingents so renowned that Egyptian pharaohs requisitioned them by name. This tradition of professional archery produces warriors of extraordinary skill.

advances.name: Makurian Horsemen
advances.text: The cavalry of Makuria patrols the Nile corridor on horseback, armed with lance and bow. These riders are the first line of defense against Bedouin incursions and foreign armies.

advances.name: Monastic Centers
advances.text: The great monasteries of Nubia (Banganarti, Ghazali, and others) serve as centers of learning, pilgrimage, and artistic production, preserving literacy in Greek, Coptic, and Old Nubian.

advances.name: Faras Cathedral Tradition
advances.text: The artistic achievements of the Faras Cathedral masters, their unique style of wall painting that blended Byzantine iconography with African humanity, represent the pinnacle of Nubian cultural expression.

event.title: The Glory of Faras
event.text: The cathedral at Faras was once the crown jewel of Christian Nubia. Its walls bore magnificent paintings, archangels with dark Nubian features, bishops in resplendent vestments, the Virgin Mary rendered in a style that blended Byzantine iconography with distinctly African sensibility. The Faras masters developed a school of art that was unique in the medieval world, where the sacred figures turned toward the mortal worshippers rather than the other way around. This tradition of artistic excellence defines Nubian cultural identity. Shall we restore Faras as a living center of faith, or honor its legacy as a beacon of learning and artistic achievement?

options.text: Restore the cathedral: let faith be our foundation.

modifiers.name: Faras Restored
modifiers.text: The cathedral at Faras has been restored as a center of Nubian Christian devotion, its walls again bearing the magnificent paintings that once awed pilgrims from across the Christian world.

options.text: The Faras masters inspire a new age of Nubian learning.

modifiers.name: Beacon of the Nile
modifiers.text: The artistic and scholarly traditions of Faras have been revived as a center of learning, where the techniques of the old masters inspire new generations of Nubian scholars and artists.

advances.name: Ivory Trade Networks
advances.text: Nubian merchants control the ivory trade from the African interior to the Mediterranean markets, operating warehouses and caravans that move this precious commodity along ancient routes.

advances.name: Desert Leathercraft
advances.text: Nubian leatherworkers transform animal hides into fine goods (saddles, shields, containers, and decorative items) using techniques perfected over generations in the desert climate.

advances.name: Court of Old Dongola
advances.text: The administrative traditions of Old Dongola, capital of Makuria for over seven centuries, provide a foundation for organized governance along the Nile.

advances.name: Legacy of the Baqt
advances.text: The Baqt, the treaty between Makuria and the Arab governors of Egypt that lasted over six centuries, established Nubia's reputation as a diplomatic power that could negotiate peace with the mightiest empires.

event.title: The Legacy of the Baqt
event.text: In 652, the kingdom of Makuria signed the Baqt with the Arab governors of Egypt, one of the longest-standing treaties in history. For over six centuries, this agreement guaranteed peace along the Nile: Nubia sent slaves, giraffes, and exotic goods northward, while Egypt provided grain, wine, and textiles in return. The Baqt was not merely a trade agreement but a diplomatic masterwork that kept the armies of the caliphate at bay when they conquered everything else in their path. This tradition of shrewd diplomacy remains part of Nubia's heritage. Shall we honor the Baqt's legacy as a diplomatic tradition, or as the foundation of our commercial networks?

options.text: The Baqt teaches us that a wise treaty is worth more than a thousand soldiers.

modifiers.name: The Baqt Tradition
modifiers.text: Nubia's diplomatic heritage, forged by the centuries-long Baqt treaty with Egypt, gives its envoys an instinctive understanding of how to negotiate from a position of cultural confidence.

options.text: The trade routes of the Baqt shall make us wealthy beyond measure.

modifiers.name: Commerce of the Baqt
modifiers.text: The trade networks established under the historic Baqt agreement continue to channel goods between sub-Saharan Africa and the Mediterranean through Nubian hands.

advances.name: Citadel Garrison
advances.text: The fortified cities of the Nile produce professional garrison troops trained in the defense of stone walls and river crossings, heavy infantry built to hold ground against any assault.

advances.name: Red Sea Incense
advances.text: The incense trade routes connecting the Horn of Africa to the Red Sea coast pass through Nubian-controlled territory, bringing fragrant wealth from distant lands. From Aydhab and Suakin the jalba, a ship sewn without a nail, carries resin and pilgrims across to Arabia.

advances.name: Nile Metalwork
advances.text:
Nubian smiths work iron and copper from the Eastern Desert into tools, weapons, and ornamental objects, supporting both agriculture and warfare along the Nile.

Available in: Nile Workshops

advances.name: Four Scripts
advances.text: Nubian scribes command four writing systems (Old Nubian, Greek, Coptic, and Arabic) giving them access to the scholarly traditions of both the Christian and Islamic worlds.

advances.name: Cataract Defenses
advances.text: The cataracts of the Nile form natural chokepoints that Nubian defenders fortify and exploit. Any army advancing up the river must pass through these deadly narrows under a rain of arrows.

advances.name: Funj Synthesis
advances.text: The Funj Sultanate created a unique cultural blend, Islamic faith layered upon African traditions, creating a Sudanese identity that transcends the boundaries of any single civilization.

event.title: The Funj Synthesis
event.text: When the Funj people rose to power in 1504, they built a new sultanate at Sennar upon the ruins of Christian Alodia. Yet the Funj did not simply replace one civilization with another. Despite adopting Islam, they preserved African customs and pre-Islamic rituals alongside their new faith. European travellers described an 'African empire with a Muslim facade', a realm where Islamic scholars taught in madrasas while traditional ceremonies continued in the countryside. This synthesis of old and new, African and Islamic, created a unique Sudanese identity. Will Nubia embrace orthodox Islamic renewal, or celebrate the syncretic heritage that makes its culture distinctive?

options.text: Let the light of true faith illuminate our land.

modifiers.name: Islamic Renewal
modifiers.text: Orthodox Islamic scholarship has taken root in Nubia, with holy men and scholars establishing schools of learning that bind the land to the wider Islamic world.

options.text: Our strength lies in the blending of traditions.

modifiers.name: Syncretic Heritage
modifiers.text: Nubia embraces its layered identity, Christian, Islamic, and African traditions woven together into a culture that transcends the boundaries of any single faith.

advances.name: Sennar Scholarship
advances.text: Under the Funj sultans the holy men of the Nile open their own schools. The masid of a learned family teaches the Quran and Maliki law, and students walk to it from across the Nile valley and beyond.

advances.name: Caravan Trade
advances.text:
Long-distance caravan routes connect Nubia to the markets of Egypt, the Horn of Africa, and the Sahel, carrying slaves, gold, and agricultural products to distant buyers. The dates of the Nile palms travel with them as wine.

Available in: Nile Workshops

advances.name: Sultanate Authority
advances.text: The Funj sultans consolidate authority over the diverse peoples of the Nile valley, imposing a centralized administration over formerly independent chieftaincies and tribal territories.

advances.name: Butana Horsemen
advances.text: The Butana steppe between the Nile and the Atbara river breeds hardy horses and fiercer riders. These mounted warriors range across the open grasslands, raiding and patrolling vast distances. The sultans of Sennar mount their mailed guard, the Black Horse, on the same breed.

advances.name: Kordofan Expansion
advances.text: Nubian authority extends westward into the highlands of Kordofan and the Nuba Mountains, incorporating new peoples and resources into the kingdom's domain.

advances.name: Sennar Musketeers
advances.text: The Funj Sultanate adopts firearms technology, equipping infantry with muskets acquired through Red Sea trade contacts. A new era of Nubian military power begins.

advances.name: Golden Age of Sennar
advances.text:
Under the late Funj sultans, Sennar reaches its peak as a thriving capital, a city of markets, mosques, and mansions where African, Arab, and Ottoman influences mingle. Lengths of its cotton cloth, the damur, pass as money in its markets.

Available in: Nile Workshops

advances.name: Blue Nile Agriculture
advances.text: The fertile lands along the Blue Nile, enriched by seasonal flooding, produce abundant harvests of grain and cotton that sustain the sultanate's growing population.

advances.name: Hamaj Regency
advances.text: The Hamaj regents who came to dominate the late Funj court bring administrative reforms that streamline governance, even as they diminish the sultans themselves to figureheads.

advances.name: Suakin Gateway
advances.text: The Red Sea port of Suakin connects Nubia to the Indian Ocean trading world, bringing wealth from the spice routes and providing access to markets across Arabia and beyond.

advances.name: Military Reform
advances.text: Late-period military reforms professionalize the Nubian army, introducing drill, standardized equipment, and tactical discipline to supplement traditional warrior courage.

advances.name: Nubian Identity
advances.text: A renewed pride in Nubian cultural identity (its unique art, language, and traditions) emerges as the foundation of a modern Nubian national consciousness.

advances.name: Modern Irrigation
advances.text: Advanced irrigation techniques transform the Nile valley, expanding the arable land far beyond what the ancient saqia could reach and supporting a growing population.

advances.name: Resistance Tradition
advances.text: Nubia has a millennia-long tradition of resisting foreign domination, from Assyria to Rome to the Arab caliphates. This defiance is not stubbornness but a deep cultural conviction that Nubian sovereignty is non-negotiable.

advances.name: Sufi Networks
advances.text: Sufi orders spread through the Nubian countryside, providing spiritual leadership, social services, and a unifying popular religion that transcends tribal and ethnic boundaries.

advances.name: Nile Mercantile
advances.text: Cross-cultural mercantile networks link Nubian traders to markets across Africa and the Middle East, creating a commercial class that spans religious and ethnic boundaries.

advances.name: Modern Governance
advances.text: Administrative modernization brings centralized record-keeping, standardized taxation, and professional bureaucracy to a kingdom that once governed through personal authority and tribal custom.

destiny.name: Destiny of Nubia
destiny.text: The Nubian lands are united once more. Whether through the bow or the trade route, the kingdom's destiny awaits.

conditions.text: Stability at least 25

event.title: The Destiny of Nubia
event.text: The Nubian kingdom stands reunited, its people proud and its borders secure. The ancient legacy of Kush, Meroe, Makuria, and Alodia lives on in every stone fortress along the Nile and every prayer in every church and mosque. Now the question turns from survival to ambition. What mark will this restored Nubia leave upon the world?

options.text: Our destiny awaits.

destiny.name: The Upper Nile Secured
destiny.text: Conquer Upper Egypt and secure the Nile corridor from the cataracts to the delta approaches. Requires ownership of Aswan and Qus, and a Nile Fortress in 3 locations.

conditions.text: Chose Land of the Bow
Own Aswan, or a subject owns it
Own Qūṣ, or a subject owns it
A Nile Fortress stands in at least 3 of our locations

event.title: The Upper Nile Secured
event.text: Nubian armies have marched north beyond the cataracts and taken Aswan and Qus. For the first time since the great pharaohs of the 25th Dynasty, Kushite soldiers stand guard over Upper Egypt. The ancient temples of Philae and Edfu, built when Nubian kings wore the double crown, are once more under the protection of a Nubian state. The fellahin of the Nile valley look up from their fields to see dark-skinned warriors whose ancestors once ruled from Memphis to Napata.

options.text: The cataracts bow before us.

destiny.name: The March Beyond
destiny.text: Extend Nubian military power into the Ethiopian highlands and the Kordofan steppe. Requires ownership of Axum and El Obeid, a Nile Fortress in 5 locations, and prestige of 50.

conditions.text: Own Axum, or a subject owns it
Own El Obeid, or a subject owns it
A Nile Fortress stands in at least 5 of our locations
Prestige at least 50

event.title: The March Beyond
event.text:
The armies of Nubia have achieved what no Nile kingdom has managed in centuries. In the west, the Kordofan steppe and its wealth of cattle and iron submit to Nubian authority. In the south, the ancient rival Axum has fallen, its mountain fortresses now garrisoned by Nubian troops. The kingdom's strategic position is formidable. It commands the Nile, the Red Sea coast, and the approaches to both Egypt and the Horn of Africa.

But the manner of our expansion defines our character. Shall we ride the fury of our warriors, pressing forward with relentless momentum? Or shall we consolidate our gains through careful logistics, building the infrastructure of lasting empire?

options.text: Fury and momentum: let nothing stand before us.

modifiers.name: Fury of the Bowmen
modifiers.text: The momentum of Nubian conquest fuels rapid reinforcement and fierce morale recovery, though the villages that send the bowmen grow weary of it.

options.text: Fortify, supply, consolidate: then advance.

modifiers.name: Logistics of Empire
modifiers.text: Efficient supply lines and rapid recruitment build a military machine that sustains expansion, though the cost of constant mobilization strains the treasury.

destiny.name: Pharaoh of Kush
destiny.text: Complete the dream of the 25th Dynasty, rule Egypt from Cairo to the sea and command the holy cities of Arabia. Requires ownership of Cairo, Alexandria and Mecca, prestige of 75, and 3,000 gold.

conditions.text: Own Cairo, or a subject owns it
Own Mecca, or a subject owns it
Own Alexandria, or a subject owns it
Prestige at least 75
Gold at least 3000

event.title: Pharaoh of Kush
event.text:
It is done. A Nubian king sits in Cairo, as Piye and Taharqa once sat in Memphis. The pyramids of Giza and the pyramids of Meroe are united under a single crown for the first time in over two thousand years. The holy city of Mecca acknowledges Nubian suzerainty. From the Mediterranean to the Red Sea, from the cataracts to the Arabian desert, a new empire has risen from the land that Egypt once called the 'wretched Kush.'

How shall the Pharaoh of Kush rule this vast domain? As a conqueror whose armies keep the peace through overwhelming force? Or as a divine ruler whose legitimacy flows from the ancient traditions of both Nubian and Egyptian kingship?

options.text: We are the conqueror: our armies are our law.

modifiers.name: Conqueror of the Nile
modifiers.text: The Pharaoh of Kush rules through overwhelming military force, maintaining cheap armies and mercenaries while declaring war at will.

options.text: We are the divine ruler of two lands.

modifiers.name: Divine Pharaoh
modifiers.text: The Pharaoh of Kush draws on ancient traditions of divine kingship, commanding the loyalty of subjects and the respect of rivals at the negotiating table.

destiny.name: The Ivory Road
destiny.text: Establish Nubia as the gateway for African ivory reaching world markets. Requires 1,000 gold, Dongola on the road down the Nile, and ivory traded in a national market.

conditions.text: Chose The Golden Corridor
Gold at least 1000
Own Dongola, or a subject owns it
A market the country is in

children.text: Ivory is produced in the market
Ivory is traded in the market

event.title: The Ivory Road
event.text: The ivory merchants of Nubia have established a commercial network that stretches from the elephant grounds of the African interior to the banking houses of the Mediterranean. Tusks that were once traded by the handful in village markets now flow through Nubian warehouses by the ton, graded, processed, and shipped to buyers across the known world. The merchants of Dongola grade and ship every tusk that comes down the river, and gold flows into Nubian coffers as surely as the Nile flows north.

options.text: The ivory roads shall make us wealthy beyond measure.

destiny.name: The Red Sea Gateway
destiny.text: Seize the port of Massawa and connect the Nile corridor to the Indian Ocean. Requires ownership of Massawa, Suakin held and built up to a development of 9, 2,000 gold, and pearls in the capital market.

conditions.text: Own Massawa, or a subject owns it
Gold at least 2000
Suakin is ours and has reached a development of 9
The capital

children.text: Pearls is produced in the market
Pearls is traded in the market

event.title: The Red Sea Gateway
event.text:
The port of Massawa is ours, and with it control of the western shore of the Red Sea. Nubia now commands both the Nile corridor and the maritime route to the Indian Ocean. Pearls from the Red Sea, spices from India, and silk from China pass through Nubian-controlled harbors alongside the ivory, gold, and incense that have always been the kingdom's stock in trade.

But the Red Sea is contested waters. Shall we invest in controlling the sea lanes themselves, building a fleet to secure our maritime commerce? Or shall we focus on making our ports the most efficient and best-connected in the region, drawing trade through institutional excellence?

options.text: Command the sea lanes: our fleet will guard our wealth.

modifiers.name: Red Sea Dominion
modifiers.text: Nubian fleets patrol the Red Sea, securing trade routes and blocking rivals, though the maritime focus leaves land forces stretched thin on the march.

options.text: Build the finest ports on the Red Sea.

modifiers.name: Port of the World
modifiers.text: Nubian ports become centers of institutional exchange and intelligence, attracting scholars and spies alike, though the cosmopolitan character erodes traditional prestige.

destiny.name: Crossroads of the World
destiny.text: Control the trade routes linking Africa, Arabia, and the Indian Ocean. Requires ownership of Jeddah and Aden, 3,000 gold, and prestige of 75.

conditions.text: Own Jeddah, or a subject owns it
Own 'Adan, or a subject owns it
Gold at least 3000
Prestige at least 75

event.title: Crossroads of the World
event.text:
Nubian traders operate in Jeddah and Aden. The kingdom that once controlled only a narrow strip of the Nile now commands the junction where African, Arabian, and Indian Ocean trade routes converge. Gold from the Eastern Desert, ivory from the interior, incense from the Horn, pearls from the Red Sea, spices from India: all pass through Nubian hands. The commercial class of Sennar and Suakin has become one of the wealthiest in the region.

Shall we extend our reach across the Indian Ocean itself, building a naval presence that projects Nubian power to distant shores? Or shall we turn inward, using our wealth to build infrastructure that makes Nubia the indispensable hub where all roads meet?

options.text: Our ships shall sail to India and beyond.

modifiers.name: Indian Ocean Reach
modifiers.text: Nubian merchantmen and warships ply the Indian Ocean, projecting power through trade and naval force across an ever-widening diplomatic network.

options.text: All roads lead through Nubia.

modifiers.name: Continental Nexus
modifiers.text: Nubia invests its trade wealth in infrastructure and integration, building a continental crossroads where goods and peoples converge at minimal cost.

units.name: Nubian Archers
units.text: The legendary bowmen of Ta-Seti, armed with great longbows of seasoned palm wood. Trained from childhood, these archers can strike targets with devastating accuracy at distances that astonish foreign observers.

units.name: Pitati Bowmen
units.text: Elite professional archers named for the Egyptian term for Nubian archer contingents. The Pitati combine the traditional Nubian mastery of the bow with organized military discipline.

units.name: Nile Horsemen
units.text: Makurian cavalry armed with lance and bow, patrolling the Nile corridor on sturdy horses. These riders are as comfortable in the saddle as on foot, able to fight as mounted archers or shock cavalry.

units.name: Dongola Guardsmen
units.text: Heavy infantry drawn from the garrison traditions of Old Dongola and the fortified Nile cities. These soldiers are trained to hold walls and river crossings against overwhelming odds.

units.name: Sennar Musketeers
units.text: Gunpowder infantry of the Funj Sultanate, equipped with muskets acquired through Red Sea trade. They represent the evolution of Nubian military tradition into the firearms age.

units.name: Jalba
units.text: A Red Sea ship whose planks are sewn with coir and caulked with shark oil, without a nail in the hull. It is loaded with pilgrims and resin far beyond what its size suggests, and it does not bear rough handling.

units.name: Black Horse
units.text: The mailed cavalry of the sultans of Sennar. Rider and horse are covered in mail and quilting, and the broadsword is carried. They are mounted on the horses of the Butana and Dongola.

buildings.name: Saqia Waterwheel
buildings.text: An ox-driven waterwheel that lifts river water to irrigate fields along the narrow Nile floodplain. The saqia is the backbone of all Nubian agriculture.

children.text: The location's raw material is Wheat
The location's raw material is Sturdy Grains
The location's raw material is Fruit

buildings.name: Nile Fortress
buildings.text: A fortified stronghold of stone and mudbrick commanding a strategic position along the Nile. These fortresses control river traffic and provide refuge against desert raiders.

buildings.name: Nubian Monastery
buildings.text: A center of Christian devotion and learning, where monks preserve manuscripts in Greek, Coptic, and Old Nubian. The monastery's scriptorium and painted chapel attract pilgrims from across the Christian world.

buildings.name: Gold Processing Camp
buildings.text: A mining camp in the Eastern Desert where gold-bearing quartz is crushed and washed. Where the land holds gold, more of the precious metal that has made Nubia wealthy since the age of the pharaohs is won from it.

where.text: The location's raw material is Gold

buildings.name: Ivory Warehouse
buildings.text: A fortified storehouse where ivory tusks from the African interior are collected, graded, and prepared for sale to Mediterranean merchants. Nubia's position on the Nile makes it the natural entrepot for this luxury trade.

buildings.name: Pottery Workshop
buildings.text: A workshop producing the distinctive painted pottery of Nubia, vessels decorated with Christian symbols and geometric patterns in a style unique to the Nile valley.

buildings.name: Masid
buildings.text: The compound of a holy family of the Funj period: a Quran school, a mosque, a guest house and the tomb of the founder, kept by his descendants. Law is taught here from the Maliki handbooks, and the students who leave it open schools of their own.

buildings.name: Nile Workshops
buildings.text: The craft quarter of a Nile town. Leather is made here first. Smiths, date wine makers and cotton weavers are added as their crafts are taken up, and each town works the craft its market can feed.

buildings.name: Coral Harbour
buildings.text: A harbour in the manner of Suakin: an island of merchants' houses built from coral blocks, reached through one channel in the reef. Pilgrim ships and the India trade are sheltered here.

buildings.name: Throne of Kush
buildings.text: A grand military command center and royal seat modeled on the ancient palaces of Napata and Meroe, from which the Pharaoh of Kush directs the armies of a restored empire.

buildings.name: Nile Emporium
buildings.text: A vast commercial complex where ivory, incense, gold, and exotic goods from three continents are traded under one roof, the jewel of Nubia's mercantile empire.

list.name: Eparchate of Nobadia
list.text: The senior provincial office of Christian Makuria, a viceroyalty governing the northern Nubadian lands from Faras and later Qasr Ibrim. The Eparch (styled 'Lord of the Mountain' in his own letters and 'domestikos' in Greek correspondence) oversaw the Egyptian frontier, regulated travel permits across the cataracts, supervised the Baqt exchange, and answered directly to the king at Old Dongola. The office is documented in Old Nubian letters and Mamluk chancery records from the 8th to 13th centuries.

list.name: Baqt Treaty System
list.text: The unique diplomatic-commercial pact concluded around 652 between Makuria and the Arab governors of Egypt, lasting more than six centuries, the longest-standing treaty between a Muslim power and a Christian state in the medieval world. An annual exchange sent slaves, ivory, and giraffes northward against grain, wine, cloth, and horses southward, conducted by salaried Nubian agents and dhimmi merchants under royal warrant. Functionally a permanent foreign-affairs ministry, the Baqt also kept a standing peace where every other Christian neighbour of the caliphate fell.

conditions.text: Stability at least 0

list.name: Faras Bishopric
list.text: The cathedral see of Pakhoras (Faras), seat of the Coptic-appointed metropolitan of Nubia. Its scriptorium produced Old Nubian liturgical manuscripts; its painted walls (archangels, nativities, and bishops in a syncretic Byzantine-African idiom recovered by archaeologists in 1961) legitimated kings and clergy alike. The bishopric administered church lands across the north, kept the calendar, and trained the literate clergy who staffed every other office of the Christian Nubian state.

conditions.text: Miaphysitism religion

list.name: Sennar Palace Administration
list.text: The Funj sultan's court at Sennar (founded 1504) was organised around the manjil heir-vizier, the qadi al-quda, and a hierarchy of palace offices staffed by jellaba slave-soldiers and Ja'aliyyin scribes. It replaced the Christian-era kingship with an Islamic absolutist court while preserving older African ceremonial. The Scottish traveller James Bruce, who reached Sennar in 1772, called it 'an African empire with a Muslim facade.'

conditions.text: Sunnism religion

list.name: Hamaj Regency
list.text: After the coup of 1761 the Hamaj regent-viziers, drawn from the Funj-Ja'aliyyin nobility, eclipsed the sultans of Sennar and ruled through a council of tribal lineage heads. The crown survived in name only; real authority devolved to the great clans of the Butana and the Ja'aliyyin confederacy. The arrangement stabilised the realm in its decline by giving the noble-tribal aristocracy a formal voice, but eroded central power until the Egyptian invasion of 1820 finished the sultanate.
